title: Hook: The Mystery of the Shepherd's Stick
text: Imagine you are walking your sheep in ancient Greece, around 4,000 years ago. A shepherd named Magnes is climbing a rocky mountain. Suddenly, the iron tip of his walking stick gets stuck to a black rock! He pulls and pulls, but the rock holds it tight. Is it magic?

title: Socratic Thinking
text: Why do you think his stick got stuck to only that specific rock, but not to the trees or the grass around him? What was special about the rock and his stick?

content.title: Discovery: The Magnetic Pull
content.description: Invisible forces pull the iron tip of the stick towards the magnetic rock.

content.definition: A natural magnetic rock. The word 'Magnet' comes from the name of the shepherd Magnes, or the place Magnesia where it was found.
A material or object that produces a magnetic field. This magnetic field is invisible but is responsible for pulling on other materials, such as iron.

question: According to legend, who discovered the first natural magnet?

title: Reflection
text: What would happen if Magnes was wearing completely leather shoes with no iron nails? Would he have discovered the magnet? Probably not! Sometimes, scientific discoveries are wonderful accidents.

content.title: Connection: Magnets in Daily Life
content.tip: Magnets aren't just rocks anymore! We use man-made magnets every day. They are in the speakers of your phone, inside your refrigerator doors, and even in some train systems like the Maglev!

content.title: Mastery Challenge: Magnet Hunt Master
content.instructions: Take a fridge magnet and walk around your house. Try sticking it to 10 different objects. Make a list of 3 things it sticks to and 3 things it doesn't stick to.

title: Hook: The Two Faces of a Magnet
text: Have you ever tried to push two magnets together and felt an invisible force pushing your hands apart? No matter how hard you push, they refuse to touch! But if you flip one magnet around, SNAP! They jump together instantly.

title: Socratic Thinking
text: Why does a magnet behave like it has two different 'personalities'? Why does it pull from one side but push from the other?

content.title: Discovery: Magnetic Poles
content.description: Opposite poles (North and South) attract each other. Like poles (North-North or South-South) repel each other.

content.definition: The regions of a magnet where the magnetic force is the strongest. Every magnet has two poles: a North pole and a South pole.
Attraction is the invisible pulling force between opposite poles. Repulsion is the invisible pushing force between like poles.

question: What happens when you bring the South pole of one magnet near the South pole of another magnet?

content.title: Reflection: The Broken Magnet Myth
content.mistake: Thinking that if you cut a magnet in half, you will get one purely North pole magnet and one purely South pole magnet.
content.correction: A magnet ALWAYS has two poles. If you cut it in half, you simply create two smaller magnets, each with its own new North and South pole!

title: Connection: Earth is a Giant Magnet!
text: Did you know the Earth itself is a giant magnet? Its magnetic field reaches far into space and protects us from dangerous solar winds. The North and South poles of our planet act just like the poles of a bar magnet. This is why a compass always points North-South!

content.title: Mastery Challenge: The Floating Paperclip
content.instructions: Tie a piece of thread to a paperclip. Tape the other end of the thread to a table. Hold a strong magnet right above the paperclip (without touching it) and pull up slightly until the thread is tight. You just made the paperclip defy gravity!
